name: Modern World History
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: Revolutions, industrialization, the world wars, decolonization and the Cold War, with causes and consequences.

lesson.intro: The modern world was shaped by a chain of upheavals: new machines, new ideas about who should rule, two world wars, and a long rivalry between superpowers. This pack follows that chain from about 1760 to 1991 and focuses on why events happened and what they changed.

sections.title: The Industrial Revolution
sections.body:
Starting in Britain around 1760, the Industrial Revolution changed how goods were made. Before it, most cloth was spun and woven by hand in homes and small workshops, the domestic system. Machines such as the spinning jenny, the water frame and later the power loom moved production into factories. James Watt's improved steam engine (patented in 1769) let factories run on coal instead of water power, and steam railways followed from the 1820s, cutting the cost of moving goods and people.

Why Britain first? Historians point to several causes working together:

- Plentiful coal and iron, often found close together
- Capital and markets from overseas trade and empire
- Farming improvements that fed a growing population and freed workers for industry
- Relatively high wages and cheap coal, which made labour-saving machines profitable
- Patents and secure property rights that rewarded invention

Consequences. Factory towns such as Manchester grew fast and were crowded and unhealthy. Children worked long hours in mills and mines until laws such as Britain's Factory Act of 1833 began to limit child labour. Workers formed trade unions, and critics such as Karl Marx attacked the new industrial capitalism. Over the long run, output per person grew faster than at any earlier time in history, and industry spread to Europe, the United States and Japan.

check.question: By the mid-1800s, what powered most British factories and railways?
choices: Electric motors and dynamos
Steam engines burning coal
Oil-fired combustion engines
Windmills and wind pumps
check.explanation: Watt's improved steam engine freed factories from rivers and water wheels, and steam locomotives drove the railways. Electricity and oil became important only later in the century and after.

sections.title: The American and French Revolutions
sections.body:
Both revolutions drew on Enlightenment ideas: that people have natural rights and that a government's authority comes from the consent of the governed.

The American Revolution. After the Seven Years' War (1756-1763), Britain was deep in debt and taxed its American colonies through measures such as the Stamp Act (1765) and the Townshend duties (1767). The colonists elected no members of Parliament, so they protested 'no taxation without representation'. Fighting began in 1775, and on 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. With French help the Americans won at Yorktown in 1781, and the Treaty of Paris (1783) recognized the United States. Its constitution, written in 1787, created a republic with separated powers.

The French Revolution. France had its own debt crisis, made worse by its costly support for the Americans. The clergy and nobility paid little tax, so the burden fell on the Third Estate, everyone else. After poor harvests pushed bread prices up, Louis XVI called the Estates-General in May 1789. The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly, and on 14 July 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen followed in August. The monarchy was abolished in 1792, the king was executed in 1793, and during the Reign of Terror tens of thousands of suspected enemies died. In 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte seized power.

Consequences: hereditary privilege was challenged across Europe, the Napoleonic Code spread equality before the law, and ideas of citizenship and nationalism shaped the century that followed.

check.question: How did France's support for the American Revolution help bring on the French Revolution?
choices: American troops invaded France to spread revolution
It persuaded Louis XVI to give up his throne
The United States demanded that France become a republic
It added heavily to the French crown's debt
check.explanation: Fighting Britain in America was expensive, and the extra debt deepened France's financial crisis in the 1780s. French soldiers returning from America also brought home ideas about liberty.

sections.title: World War I: causes and outcomes
sections.body:
Historians often group the long-term causes of World War I under four headings:

- Militarism: an arms race, including the Anglo-German naval race, and rigid war plans
- Alliances: the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain faced the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (Italy stayed neutral in 1914 and joined the Allies in 1915)
- Imperialism: rivalry over colonies and influence
- Nationalism: national pride and grievances, especially among the Slavic peoples of the Balkans

The trigger came on 28 June 1914, when Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia mobilized to support Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and Germany's invasion of neutral Belgium brought Britain in on 4 August.

Germany's plan for a quick victory failed, and the Western Front settled into trench warfare. The United States joined the Allies in 1917, while revolution in Russia led it to leave the war in early 1918. The fighting ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.

Outcomes:

- More than 8 million soldiers and millions of civilians died.
- Four empires collapsed, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, and new states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared.
- The Treaty of Versailles (1919) made Germany accept responsibility for the war (the 'war guilt' clause), pay reparations, give up land and all its colonies, and limit its army to 100,000 men.
- The League of Nations was created to keep the peace, but the United States never joined.

check.question: What was the Schlieffen Plan?
choices: A British plan to blockade Germany's North Sea ports
Russia's plan to strike Austria-Hungary before Germany could help
Germany's plan to beat France fast via Belgium, then face Russia
An American peace plan based on national self-determination
check.explanation: Expecting a two-front war, Germany planned to knock France out quickly by marching through Belgium. The plan stalled at the Marne in September 1914, leading to trench stalemate, and the invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war.

sections.title: Between the wars and World War II
sections.body:
The peace did not last. Many Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles. Hyperinflation in 1923 wiped out savings, and after the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 the Great Depression brought mass unemployment around the world. Desperate voters turned to extremists. Mussolini had already taken power in Italy in 1922. In Germany the Nazi Party became the largest in parliament in 1932, and Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933.

The League of Nations could not stop aggression. It had no army, needed its members to agree on sanctions, and lacked the United States. It did little when Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) or Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935). Britain and France followed a policy of appeasement, giving in to some of Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding war. At Munich in 1938 they accepted Germany's takeover of the Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia. When Germany seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, appeasement ended. After signing a non-aggression pact with the Soviet Union, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war two days later.

Turning points: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941; Japan attacked the US base at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941; the Soviet victory at Stalingrad (1943) and the D-Day landings in Normandy (June 1944) pushed Germany back. Germany surrendered in May 1945. Japan surrendered in August 1945, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet declaration of war.

An estimated 70 to 85 million people died, most of them civilians. In the Holocaust, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of others.

check.question: What brought the United States into World War II as a combatant?
choices: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941
Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939
The sinking of the liner Lusitania by a U-boat
The fall of France to Germany in June 1940
check.explanation: The US stayed out of the fighting until Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941; Germany declared war on the US four days later. The Lusitania was sunk in 1915, during World War I.

sections.title: After 1945: the UN, decolonization, the Cold War and the EU
sections.body:
The United Nations was founded in 1945 (its charter took effect on 24 October) to prevent another world war. Learning from the League, it gave five main victors, the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, permanent seats on the Security Council with a veto, so the great powers would stay inside the system.

Decolonization. Between 1945 and the 1970s most colonies in Asia and Africa became independent. The war had weakened Britain, France and the Netherlands, independence movements had grown stronger, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, in a partition that uprooted millions. In 1960 alone, 17 African countries gained independence. Some transitions were peaceful; others, such as Algeria's war against France (1954-1962), were long and violent. Borders drawn by colonial powers often left lasting conflicts.

The Cold War. From about 1947 to 1991 the United States and its allies faced the Soviet Union and its allies: capitalist democracy against one-party communism. The US followed a policy of containment, trying to stop communism spreading. The rivals built alliances (NATO in 1949, the Warsaw Pact in 1955) and nuclear arsenals. Because a direct war could destroy both, they competed through proxy wars such as Korea and Vietnam, the space race and propaganda. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought them closest to nuclear war.

The end came quickly. Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, began reforms and chose not to use force to hold Eastern Europe. In 1989 its communist governments fell, and the Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November. Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

European integration. To make another war between France and Germany practically impossible, six countries pooled their coal and steel in the European Coal and Steel Community (1951). The Treaty of Rome (1957) created the European Economic Community, and the Maastricht Treaty (signed in 1992) founded the European Union.

check.question: In which year did the Soviet Union dissolve?
check.explanation: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. In 1989 the Berlin Wall opened, in 1985 Gorbachev came to power, and in 1961 the Wall was built.

keyTerms.definition: Production in large buildings where workers ran machines driven by water or steam, replacing work done at home.
An 18th-century movement that stressed reason, natural rights and government by consent.
Strong loyalty to one's nation and the belief that each nation should govern itself.
Payments a defeated country must make for war damage, as Germany was required to after 1919.
Giving in to an aggressor's demands to avoid war, as Britain and France did with Hitler in the 1930s.
The process by which colonies became independent states, mostly between 1945 and the 1970s.
The US Cold War policy of stopping communism from spreading to new countries.
A conflict in which rival powers back opposing sides instead of fighting each other directly.

summary: The Industrial Revolution, starting in Britain around 1760, moved work into factories, grew cities and began sustained economic growth.
The American (1776) and French (1789) Revolutions spread the ideas that power comes from the people and that citizens have rights.
World War I grew out of alliances, militarism, imperialism and nationalism, and the 1919 peace left resentment that helped cause World War II.
The Great Depression and the League of Nations' weakness let aggressive regimes expand until war broke out in 1939.
After 1945 the UN, decolonization, the Cold War and European integration reshaped the world; the Cold War ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how the way World War I ended helped lead to World War II, using at least two concrete links between them.

questions.question: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain rather than elsewhere?
choices: Its government designed, built and ran the first factories itself
It had the largest population and cheapest labour in Europe
Coal, trade capital, big markets and high wages made machines pay off
It imported cheap steam engines that had been invented in France
questions.explanation: Historians stress a combination: accessible coal and iron, capital and markets from trade, a growing population fed by better farming, and wages that were high compared with the price of coal, which made labour-saving machines profitable. British labour was relatively expensive, not cheap, and private entrepreneurs, not the state, built the factories.

questions.question: Explain how the move from the domestic system to the factory system changed workers' lives.
questions.answer: Work moved from homes and small workshops into factories with machines driven by water or steam. Workers earned wages for long, fixed hours set by the factory clock and crowded into fast-growing towns, conditions that led in time to trade unions and laws such as Britain's 1833 Factory Act.
questions.explanation: The factory system concentrated machines, workers and power in one place. Output rose, but where and how people lived and worked changed, and those conditions drove the first labour laws and unions.

questions.question: In what year did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explanation: The Declaration was adopted on 4 July 1776, a year after fighting began in 1775. Britain recognized American independence only in the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

questions.question: What was the main grievance behind the American colonists' slogan 'No taxation without representation'?
choices: The colonies paid far higher taxes than people living in Britain
Parliament taxed the colonies, but they elected no members to it
Colonists were being drafted to fight Britain's wars in Europe
France was imposing taxes on American trade with Britain
questions.explanation: Colonists objected that Parliament, where they had no members, was imposing taxes such as the Stamp Act. They actually paid less tax than people in Britain; the dispute was about consent, not the size of the bill.

questions.question: In what year did Parisians storm the Bastille, an event often used to mark the start of the French Revolution?
questions.explanation: The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789, about two months after Louis XVI had called the Estates-General. France still celebrates 14 July as its national day.

questions.question: Which combination of pressures led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789?
choices: A Protestant revolt demanding freedom of worship
Defeat in the Napoleonic Wars and foreign occupation
A demand by peasants to restore the old feudal dues
Heavy royal debt, an unfair tax system and costly bread
questions.explanation: The crown was close to bankruptcy, partly from wars including its support for the Americans; the clergy and nobility paid little tax; and poor harvests had pushed bread prices up. The Napoleonic Wars came later, after Napoleon took power in 1799.

questions.question: What was the immediate trigger of World War I?
choices: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914
Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939
The sinking of the passenger liner Lusitania in 1915
The Russian Revolution and the fall of the Tsar in 1917
questions.explanation: On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist killed the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia a month later. The invasion of Poland started World War II, and the Lusitania sinking and the Russian Revolution came after World War I had begun.

questions.question: Why did a conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia turn into a war across Europe within about a week?
choices: Serbia launched surprise invasions of both Germany and France
Alliance ties pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain in turn
The League of Nations ordered all of its members to take sides
All of Europe's monarchs agreed to declare war on the same day
questions.explanation: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary and declared war on Russia and France, and Germany's invasion of Belgium brought Britain in. The League of Nations did not exist until 1920.

questions.question: Which was a term of the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?
choices: Germany received Alsace-Lorraine from France
Germany was allowed to keep its overseas colonies
Germany accepted blame for the war and agreed to pay reparations
Germany became a founding member of the League of Nations
questions.explanation: Article 231, the 'war guilt' clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the war's damage, which justified reparations. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France and all its colonies, and it was not admitted to the League until 1926.

questions.question: Which development did most to help extremist parties such as the Nazis win mass support in Germany in the early 1930s?
choices: Mass unemployment and poverty during the Great Depression
A rapid rise in wages and exports after 1929
The Allies' decision to cancel all reparations in 1919
Germany's success in gaining new colonies in Africa
questions.explanation: After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, American loans dried up and German unemployment rose to about six million by 1932. Desperate voters turned to parties promising radical change, and the Nazis became the largest party in parliament in 1932. Reparations were imposed in 1919, not cancelled.

questions.question: What name is given to the policy Britain and France followed in the 1930s of giving in to some of Hitler's demands to avoid war?
questions.explanation: Appeasement peaked with the Munich Agreement of 1938, which let Germany take the Sudetenland. It ended when Germany seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939.

questions.question: Why did the League of Nations fail to stop aggression in the 1930s?
choices: Its own army was too small to fight Japan and Italy at once
It was dissolved soon after the Wall Street Crash of 1929
Germany and Italy used vetoes on its Security Council
It had no army, depended on agreement, and lacked the United States
questions.explanation: The League could only call for sanctions, which members often ignored, and the United States never joined. It did little when Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 or Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935. A Security Council with vetoes belongs to the later United Nations.
questions.concept: failure of the League of Nations

questions.question: How did the founders of the United Nations try to avoid the League of Nations' main weakness?
choices: They gave the UN a large permanent army of its own
They kept the defeated powers and the Soviet Union out
They required every member to agree before any action
They gave the great powers permanent Security Council vetoes
questions.explanation: The League failed partly because great powers stayed out or left. The UN gave five main victors permanent seats and a veto so they would stay inside the system. The UN has no standing army of its own, and the Soviet Union was a founding member.

questions.question: Which factor helped speed up decolonization after 1945?
choices: World War II had weakened the European colonial powers
Colonies had become more profitable than ever before
The UN Charter required colonies to stay under European rule
Both superpowers strongly supported Europe's empires
questions.explanation: Britain, France and the Netherlands came out of the war exhausted and in debt, while independence movements had grown stronger. The UN Charter supported self-determination, and both the US and the Soviet Union opposed old-style empires.

questions.question: Explain why the Cold War is called 'cold'.
questions.answer: The United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly. Nuclear weapons made a direct war potentially suicidal for both, so they competed through an arms race, the space race, rival alliances, propaganda and proxy wars such as Korea and Vietnam.
questions.explanation: 'Cold' means no direct fighting between the superpowers. The rivalry was still deadly in proxy wars, and in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 it came close to nuclear war.

questions.question: In what year was the Berlin Wall opened, as communist governments in Eastern Europe fell?
questions.explanation: The Wall opened on 9 November 1989. Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, ending the Cold War.

questions.question: What was the original aim of the European Coal and Steel Community, founded in 1951?
choices: To replace national currencies with a single European money
To bind France and Germany together so war between them became impossible
To form a military alliance of Western Europe against the Soviet Union
To give Britain control of Europe's coal and steel supplies
questions.explanation: Coal and steel were the raw materials of war, so putting them under shared control tied France, West Germany and four neighbours together. The euro came decades later, the Western military alliance was NATO, and Britain did not join until 1973.
